text:
Mathematics and Elite Squad Dynamics
A Modest Proposal for the Improvement of American Civilization Through Grand Theft Auto VI
Being an earnest inquiry into the moral, economic, and technological benefits of spending thirteen years constructing a virtual Florida in which Americans may commit the crimes they are too exhausted to commit in the actual one.

November 19, 2026 — Launch Day

By our Special Correspondent for Applied Degeneracy, Digital Economics, and the Collapse of Western Civilization

It is with considerable satisfaction that I announce the arrival of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest triumph of American ingenuity, in which a civilization possessing the means to simulate entire metropolitan areas has elected to devote those means to stealing automobiles, shooting policemen, and purchasing trousers.

The enterprise has consumed thirteen years.

This is approximately the length of time required to educate a physician, establish a successful agricultural cooperative, or bring a moderately incompetent infrastructure project to its second environmental-impact assessment.

Rockstar Games, however, has employed this period to achieve something arguably more ambitious: Florida, but with functioning collision detection.

I consider this a remarkable accomplishment, particularly as the original Florida has thus far resisted such an improvement.
I. Concerning the Present Scarcity of Meaningful Employment
There are, by some accounts, millions of young men in the United States who feel alienated from the economy, isolated from society, and disenchanted with the promises of capitalism.

Fortunately, an international consortium of computer programmers has found an answer.

They shall become car thieves.

Not actual car thieves, of course, for that would inconvenience the insurance industry and occasion considerable police attention. Rather, they shall purchase expensive computing equipment, subscribe to high-speed internet services, and engage in imaginary car theft under conditions carefully negotiated by corporate lawyers.

They shall experience liberty.

They shall experience rebellion.

They shall experience the exhilarating freedom of driving a stolen Lamborghini directly into a municipal fountain, after which they shall purchase a new pair of virtual sunglasses.

And what better emblem of the modern American spirit could there be than a man who has spent eighty dollars for permission to disobey laws that do not exist?

The criminal of the eighteenth century had at least the satisfaction of depriving a wealthy gentleman of his property.

The criminal of the twenty-first century must first purchase his own copy of the wealthy gentleman's property, agree to its terms of service, and occasionally download an update.

Thus has capitalism accomplished what two centuries of law enforcement could not: it has made robbery profitable for the person being robbed.
II. A Wonderful New Species of Rebellion
I am particularly delighted by the philosophical sophistication of the enterprise.

The game is a satire of American consumer culture, financed by an enormously successful corporation, distributed through multinational technology platforms, and marketed through one of the most extravagant exercises in consumer anticipation ever devised.

It condemns materialism.

It offers an Ultimate Edition.

It mocks our obsession with brands.

It has a merchandise store.

It exposes the hollow promises of consumer capitalism.

It would be grateful if you subscribed.

I cannot imagine a more perfect arrangement. Indeed, I propose that the Smithsonian immediately establish a permanent exhibition dedicated to the subject, entitled:

THE REVOLUTION WILL BE MONETIZED.

Admission: $79.99.

Gift-shop access requires the Ultimate Edition.
III. Of the Peculiar Customs of the People of Leonida
The fictional state of Leonida, we are assured, bears a striking resemblance to Florida.

I have examined this proposition with considerable care.

Leonida contains criminals, swamps, alligators, aspiring celebrities, extravagant wealth, conspiratorial thinking, astonishingly poor judgment, and people who regard the operation of motor vehicles as a competitive contact sport.

Florida contains these things also.

The principal distinction appears to be that in Leonida, a computer must labor intensely to produce such phenomena, whereas in Florida they arise spontaneously from the interaction of sunlight, alcohol, and municipal zoning regulations.

This suggests a fascinating scientific question.

If a simulation becomes sufficiently faithful to Florida, does it eventually develop its own homeowners' association?

And if so, can the association be defeated with a rocket launcher?

I submit this as a suitable subject for doctoral research.

The developers have reportedly constructed an enormous world of beaches, highways, neighborhoods, businesses, wildlife, weather, and intricate human behavior.

Here is an opportunity for unprecedented artistic achievement.

The human player may encounter the complexity of an entire civilization.

He may examine its inequalities, confront its moral contradictions, explore its architecture, and investigate the subtle interplay between personal freedom and institutional power.

Or he may hit a pedestrian with a golf cart.

I predict the latter will receive considerable scholarly attention.
IV. Concerning Two Young Persons of Questionable Character
Our protagonists are Jason and Lucia, two young people seeking prosperity in a society whose economic opportunities have largely been monopolized by persons already possessing prosperity.

They are, in other words, entrepreneurs.

Their business model differs from that of Silicon Valley principally in that their thefts are represented directly on the screen.

A venture capitalist might observe that the pair have a compelling founding story, strong execution capability, excellent geographical market penetration, and an unusually aggressive customer-acquisition strategy.

Their principal deficiency is that they have not yet described their enterprise as artificial intelligence.

This may be remedied.

I propose a startup called CrimeGPT, whose purpose is to automate the commission of virtual felonies, thereby liberating the player to pursue higher-order activities such as reading quarterly shareholder reports.

Its seed round shall be $400 million.

Its product shall be an animated button labeled STEAL CAR.

Its founders shall describe it as transformational.

They will not be wrong.
V. An Inquiry Into the Extraordinary Patience of the Gaming Public
Thirteen years.

Permit me to dwell upon this figure.

Thirteen years is an age at which a child may begin to develop independent moral reasoning.

A child born on the release date of Grand Theft Auto V is now old enough to ask why his father has spent the greater part of his adult life awaiting its sequel.

The father will explain that the new game possesses more realistic reflections, improved pedestrian behavior, and substantially greater fidelity in the depiction of automotive upholstery.

The child will naturally ask whether these advances have improved civilization.

The father will say that he does not know, but that the water looks absolutely incredible.

And it does.

We have reached the extraordinary stage of technical progress at which a simulated puddle may require more computational effort than the entire Apollo guidance computer, while serving the equally noble purpose of reflecting the undercarriage of a stolen pickup truck.

I shall not criticize this allocation of resources.

I merely suggest that NASA should have considered giving Neil Armstrong a wanted level.
VI. The Internet, Having Finally Met Its Natural Enemy
Today, November 19, 2026, the game has arrived.

According to contemporary reporting, its download is approximately 212 gigabytes.
AP News+1

This is a remarkable quantity of information to transmit for the purpose of enabling a man to drive badly.

Internet providers have been obliged to prepare for the consequent demand.

Somewhere, at this very moment, a network engineer is gazing at a wall of flashing equipment and contemplating the civilization that has entrusted him with its infrastructure.

He has studied mathematics.

He has studied telecommunications.

He understands packet switching, congestion control, redundancy, and the statistical properties of network traffic.

He knows that the internet might facilitate universal education, international scientific cooperation, and the free exchange of human knowledge.

Instead, seven hundred thousand men are simultaneously attempting to download the same simulated strip club.

The engineer reaches for his coffee.

The router begins blinking.

And so, perhaps, does God.
VII. A Few Words Concerning the Moral Improvement of Youth
Critics of the franchise have long argued that games of this nature encourage antisocial behavior.

This criticism, though doubtless sincere, seems to overlook the remarkable degree of social discipline required to participate in the modern gaming economy.

The average customer must:
Obey the platform's rules.
Maintain an account in good standing.
Accept the publisher's licensing conditions.
Preserve sufficient disk space.
Remain connected to the relevant services where required.
Refrain from certain prohibited forms of misconduct.
Having fulfilled these obligations, he may then enjoy the thrilling fantasy of being an individual who refuses to obey rules.

Thus, the modern criminal imagination is now cultivated in a carefully regulated commercial environment.

It is as though Robin Hood had been required to enroll in a loyalty program before entering Sherwood Forest.

There are rewards.

There are incentives.

There may be exclusive seasonal benefits.

The outlaw has become an account holder.

The revolution has a customer-support department.
VIII. The Great Philosophical Discovery
There is, however, one feature of this phenomenon that troubles me deeply.

For decades, artists, philosophers, educators, and political reformers have struggled to persuade the public to examine the absurdities of modern American life.

They have written books.

They have produced documentaries.

They have organized demonstrations.

They have delivered lectures upon the moral bankruptcy of consumerism, the corrupting influence of wealth, the theatrical nature of celebrity, and the increasing difficulty of distinguishing public life from commercial entertainment.

Most have been ignored.

Rockstar Games has discovered a superior method.

It has constructed a colossal satire of the very same society, placed a stolen automobile in the foreground, and sold tickets to the experience.

Millions have arrived.

This represents a devastating indictment of the literary profession.

Jonathan Swift spent years fashioning arguments of exquisite irony and moral precision.

He might have achieved vastly greater commercial success had he included a minimap and a button for punching horses.

Indeed, A Modest Proposal itself might have enjoyed an altogether different reception under the title:

GRAND THEFT IRELAND: THE POTATO HEIST.

Downloadable content: The Landlord Expansion.
IX. My Own Modest Proposal
Having considered the matter, I believe the franchise has not yet gone far enough.

Its developers should cease representing American society through satire and instead reproduce the institutions of American life with absolute fidelity.

I therefore recommend the following features for Grand Theft Auto VII.

The player shall begin with $47,000 in student debt.

His principal antagonist shall be a health-insurance company.

The wanted-level system shall be replaced by a credit score.

Successful criminal enterprises shall obtain venture financing, become too large to fail, and acquire their competitors.

The final mission shall involve navigating a customer-service telephone tree.

A player wishing to purchase property shall be required to demonstrate three years of stable income and provide documentation of previous rental history.

Police pursuit shall be suspended whenever the player enters a sufficiently expensive neighborhood.

The protagonist's automobile shall depreciate immediately upon purchase.

The player shall be unable to progress to the next mission until a state agency processes his application.

And the ultimate achievement, accessible only after approximately 400 hours of play, shall be called:

HOMEOWNERSHIP.

Upon unlocking it, the player shall receive a notification that his property taxes have increased.

This, I submit, would be a truly adult video game.
X. A Final Consideration of the Human Condition
The genius of Grand Theft Auto is not that it allows its players to escape the world.

It is that it persuades them to purchase a second world that is even more ridiculous than the first, while congratulating themselves on having recognized the ridiculousness.

There is something almost tender about this arrangement.

We have built machines capable of calculating the motions of galaxies, modeling molecular interactions, and examining the most delicate structures of mathematical logic.

We connect them across a planetary communications network whose existence would have seemed supernatural to nearly every human being who ever lived.

And what do we do?

We simulate Florida.

Not because we are obliged to.

Not because Florida is in danger of extinction.

Not because the real Florida has become inaccessible, although this possibility cannot be entirely dismissed.

We do it because the simulated Florida permits us to commit atrocities without consequence, acquire wealth without labor, and inhabit a world where the moral bankruptcy of society is at least accompanied by an excellent soundtrack.

And we call it entertainment.

I cannot say whether this represents the pinnacle of human civilization or the moment at which civilization quietly excused itself from the room.

But I am inclined to believe that future archaeologists, examining the surviving data centers of our age, will conclude that we worshipped a peculiar deity called Rockstar, who appeared once every thirteen years, demanded considerable tribute, and rewarded the faithful with increasingly realistic representations of asphalt.

They will marvel at our ingenuity.

They will mourn our priorities.

And somewhere in the ruins, a server will still be attempting to verify a license.

Editorial conclusion
It is difficult to remain entirely pessimistic.

For all its absurdities, humanity has finally achieved something philosophers have sought since antiquity:

A world in which crime pays, death is temporary, and the laws of physics can be defeated by driving a motorcycle up a staircase.

The price of admission is reasonable, provided one does not count the console, the broadband service, the additional storage, the electricity, the optional premium benefits, and the thirteen years of one's mortal existence spent waiting.

We may therefore proclaim with confidence that the future has arrived.

It is beautiful.

It is grotesque.

It is available for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.
And the internet is blinking.

God help us all.

Mathematics and Elite Squad Dynamics

All bullshit is welcome. Unlabeled bullshit is not.

Editorial disclosure: This is satire, not a gameplay review. The release date, setting, characters, and launch details are grounded in Rockstar's November 19 announcement and official game materials. The proposed features, institutions, and philosophical diagnoses are products of the author's increasingly reasonable despair.

Global News Brief  

1. HI News: Surgeons at Jerusalem’s Hadassah Hospital Ein Kerem performed Israel’s first spinal surgery using Medtronic’s AI-assisted Stealth AXiS system, treating Shani, an 18-year-old dancer with severe scoliosis. Led by Dr. Joshua Schroeder, the team used advanced planning and precision navigation during the five-hour-plus operation. Within a week, Shani was walking upright without her previous pain and returned home to begin physiotherapy.

2. Washington Post: About 1 in 9 American adults now take a GLP-1 drug, according to a recent Gallup poll. These medications, including Ozempic and Wegovy, mimic a hormone that helps regulate blood sugar and appetite, treating diabetes and aiding weight loss. A new study found that weight training during treatment improved strength despite preserving little muscle, highlighting its benefits for physical function. https://t.co/Zejbt0xgfQ

3. PBS: Iran targeted the U.S. Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain on November 18, apparently retaliating for an American strike on a Revolutionary Guard missile site on Qeshm Island. Kuwait and Bahrain reported intercepting the attacks, with no immediate details of casualties or damage. The exchanges heightened fears of renewed regional conflict and prompted intensified diplomatic efforts to prevent escalation.

4. Middle East Monitor: Ireland’s national police force purchased drone-jamming and tracking systems from Israeli company Sentrycs earlier in 2026, despite the government’s 2024 pledge to stop buying Israeli military equipment. The systems are installed on rooftops overlooking diplomatic venues, raising questions about whether the police purchase falls within the procurement restrictions.

5. L.A. Times: More than 7,000 Los Angeles Unified students walked out of class on Nov. 16 to protest federal immigration raids and deportations, according to an unnamed school police source cited by the Los Angeles Times. The district had yet to release an official count. Students called for an end to ICE raids and urged the district to expand Dream Centers, which offer legal guidance, mental health care, food, and clothing, from 19 high schools to every campus. Police described the demonstrations as largely peaceful and reported a brief scuffle near the downtown federal building and some property damage.

6. Financial Times: Gold fell to $3,742 a troy ounce on Wednesday, its lowest since September 2025 and about a third below its January record of $5,595. The metal has dropped 10% since U.S. stocks peaked in early October, leading investors to question its role as a safe haven during the tech sell-off. Higher interest rates have made gold, which pays no yield, less attractive, and some analysts suspect investors sold it to cover losses in tech stocks. Some remain positive about gold’s longer-term outlook, citing continued central bank buying and rising government debt.

7. NY Post: Anthropic shares closed their first day of trading at $97.17, up from the $83 IPO price, valuing the company at roughly $1.7 trillion. The average employee’s stake was estimated at $44 million on paper. The Hill estimated that about 2,800 of Anthropic’s 5,000 employees held at least $10 million in equity, including 600 non-founders with stakes worth $100 million or more.

8. Reuters: Russia flew two Tu-95 strategic bombers and two refuelling aircraft to Da Nang, Vietnam, after their passage near Japan and Taiwan drew concern from both. text:
Growth of Backyard Ultra

-The sport has grown extremely fast since Sam and Phil Gore first broke the 100-loop barrier in 2023.
- In 2022 only two athletes (Mirin & Evo) had done 100+; by the time of this recording roughly 20 men had reached 100 loops.
- Entry standards for Big’s have risen sharply—from ~60–61 loops on the at-large list a few years ago to an expected 90s qualifier by 2027.
- The format’s fixed loop + fixed start time makes it far easier to film and follow than traditional point-to-point ultras, which has helped drive media interest (Go One More, Last Soul Ultra, etc.).

Sam’s Background

- Grew up in New Zealand playing rugby and boxing; later moved to Nashville to play and coach rugby.
- Realized he was naturally better suited to endurance than contact sports and gradually dropped rugby, boxing, triathlon, and mountain biking to focus solely on running.
- Ultra progression: first 50K (2018), 100K (2019), 100-mile (2020), first backyard ultra (2021, NZ record), then went all-in professionally in 2022.

Injury Experiences (especially Achilles)

- During the 118/119-loop world-record attempt with Phil Gore, Sam tore both Achilles tendons (roughly 2 cm tears) after ~50 hours and continued for another ~68 hours on the injuries.
- Rehab was conservative (no boot); he was limited for months, pulled out of UTMB, and arrived at the following Big’s still compromised (managed only ~100 miles).
- He took a long intentional break from backyard ultras afterward to recover physically and mentally; by the next Teams Championship he felt excited again rather than traumatized.

What Actually Limits Performance

- Sam’s view: desire and willingness to keep pushing usually stop people long before true mechanical breakdown.
- Most athletes (even strong ones) quit within hours of the first significant struggle rather than grinding all the way to catastrophic injury.
- Small mistakes compound over multi-day efforts—nutrition, a bit of gravel in a shoe, aggressive massage-gun use, untested shoes, downhill eccentric loading, etc.
- Being both tough and fast is a major advantage: faster runners bank more rest between loops and can stay efficient deep into the race, whereas slower runners are already “toughing it out” from day one.

Coaching & Development

- Sam coaches a range of athletes from beginners to elites using the same core methodologies he uses on himself.
- Success stories include taking Kendall from not breaking 20 min for 5K to a 72-loop PB, and others making large jumps (e.g., 60s to 93 loops).
- Desire and commitment matter more than a traditional running résumé; some athletes with modest backgrounds progress rapidly if they fully buy in, while others with better résumés flop.
- Event experience is valuable but not everything—high mileage for durability + correct race-day execution in the tent and on the loop are the bigger levers.

Professional Side & Sponsorships

- Sam was one of the first (possibly the first) to go fully professional primarily through backyard ultra.
- He has largely monetized via coaching rather than traditional brand deals, which has given him more autonomy.
- He is now exploring more sponsorships (shoes, apparel, sunglasses) and has a camera person who handles content so he can focus on training and racing.

Structure, Rules & Team Championship

- Prefers keeping the rules simple and minimizing gray areas (traditionalist view on phones, crew contact, etc.).
- The Teams Championship (born during COVID as virtual country-vs-country events) is now the main golden-ticket path to Big’s for most athletes.
- Sam has won it for New Zealand three years in a row and is considering stepping aside in future years so other NZ athletes can compete for the golden ticket without having to beat him.
- Notes the psychological effect: when a dominant athlete is absent, the rest of a national team can sometimes go deeper because second place suddenly feels winnable.

2027 Outlook

- Planned calendar includes Last Soul Ultra (Tennessee, Feb), Go One More (Austin, May), Last Soul World Series Final (Germany, Aug), and Big’s (Oct).
- Expects multiple 100+ loop efforts; historically almost no one has done three or four 100s in a single year.
- Believes clean 100-loop efforts are repeatable with decent recovery; stacking 120–140+ loops (especially if injured during the race) is a different proposition.
- Overall tone is that 2027 will be a defining year as more top athletes repeatedly meet at the same high-stakes events.

Congressman-elect Brent Taylor Names David Pair as District Director

Franklin, TN — Congressman-elect Brent Taylor announced the appointment of David Pair as District Director. Pair brings extensive experience in government affairs, legislative outreach, and local public service in Williamson County and across Tennessee.

text:
Perry’s Perspective – The Lie Is The Point
It says on our coins “In God We Trust.” It should now say “A Country of Political Will.”
Justice seems to be optional. Justice is rarely applied if you are a Democrat. Republicans face it all the time. The difference is political will. Democrats have it. They use it. Republicans, especially in the Senate refuse to play offense. Their political will exists, but never at a dose strong enough to bring results. It is about as strong as children’s aspirin. They manage. They negotiate. They wait for the perfect case and the perfect optics and then explain why the moment passed.
A joke on the golf course is that it is easier to ask for forgiveness than to get permission. In government the forgiveness part is optional. So is the correction. You open the border, you pass the bill that raises healthcare costs (Obamacare), you name the inflation act after the problem it makes worse (Inflation Reduction Act), and then you move on. The mistake stays. The people who made it stay. The next cycle starts from the new floor, doubling down on the mistakes.
We are not a country of laws. We are a country of political will. The will to open the border or the will to close it. The will to remove the people who came in illegally or the will to decide the optics are too hard and call the decision mercy.
Fourteen to eighteen million were let in under the last administration. Maybe three million have been removed. That is the trade. Who does not take that trade every day of the week if the only cost is a press conference and a promise to do better next time? The caravans are already forming again. The same route, the same organizations, the same calculation that the door will be open long enough and the removal will never match the entry. Democrats get to break the law in public. Republicans get to manage the consequences in private and then explain why full reversal is unrealistic.
Trump and some Republicans are now hinting at middle ground for people who have been here a long time and contribute. Any candidate who runs on that suggestion will be finished with the base. The base watched the numbers. They watched the hospitals, the schools, the wage pressure, the fraud cases. They are not interested in a negotiated settlement that leaves most of the fourteen million in place and calls the remainder a success. If removal is too messy for the optics, then the alternatives must be real. Tax the activity until staying is more expensive than leaving. Make the benefits unavailable. Make the jobs unavailable. Make the paperwork a wall. If you cannot deport, make it impossible to stay. That is still a policy. Pretending the problem solves itself is not.
The best way out is always through. Removal will be messy. Spanish-speaking communities know people who are here illegally. The midterms showed their support drop. None of that changes the arithmetic or the precedent. The other side is committed to a view of the country that treats the border as a suggestion and citizenship as a feeling. They do not apologize for it. They do not soften it after a bad cycle. They expand it. If they win in 2028 the fourteen to eighteen million will be the opening bid. Another fourteen million and Texas is permanently blue.
The question is whether the people who claim to oppose that view are willing to stay committed to their own when the cameras are on and the numbers are ugly. A majority of Republicans have shown they will not play offense. The base is going to have to decide whether that is acceptable or support only those that do.
Todd Erzan’s line is the right one: the lie is the point. The lie that the numbers are manageable. The lie that long-term presence equals assimilation. The lie that welfare and fraud are side effects instead of the mechanism. The truth is replacement.
A solution still needs to be said out loud to the people whose feelings do not care about the facts. The facts are the entry numbers, the removal numbers, and the knowledge that the next administration that treats the border as optional will not be interested in cleaning up the last one. The will to reverse it has to exist before the next election, not after. Otherwise, the coins can keep the old motto. The reality already matches the new one. A half-dose of will was never going to reverse a full-dose of commitment.

You know, his want to, his level of physicality, and then what are they good at, and how do we put them in position to be successful? And then the players' understanding that, hey, we think you can be really good at this, and let's give this a shot. Let's put all our chips over here. And after the first year, maybe that's not the best fit. Maybe it's shifting over here. But I think that comes with trust, and then trusting us in that, hey, we're going to find you a role. You're committed to the program. You're working hard in the off-season. You're doing well in school. You've got a skill set that we think we can utilize in a way that, if it gives us 5,10, 15,20 snaps a game, whatever that looks like, we're going to try to find a way to reward you, in essence, for what you're giving to the program."

On Terry's growth this year:

"Well, we use a simple saying around here: a job well done is an opportunity to do more. He's done a good job for us. You know, when he's been put in and called to action early on, he's performed well, and then he got an opportunity to do more, and then he got a couple more carries, and then he caught a big pass on a third-down conversion last week. So his role is growing. You know, naturally, he's a really good presence for us on third down and pass protection. He's a big body. He's tough to get around in blitz situations. He's a good chipper and helper for the offensive line because he has a presence that way. But at the same time, got to remember when he first got here, he's playing wide receiver. Host: An historic judgment from the International Court of Justice today, ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority. Stephanie Sy details how the ruling comes years after Myanmar's Muslim minority was forced to flee. And a warning. This report contains images that some viewers may find disturbing.

Stephanie Sy: Today, a sliver of justice for the Rohingya Muslims of Myanmar.

Judge: The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group.

Stephanie Sy: The landmark nine-to-six decision is the first of its kind. Before today, the International Court of Justice, a United Nations body, had never held a state responsible for genocide.

Judge: The only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group, namely the Rohingya population in Northern Rakhine State.

Stephanie Sy: Today's ruling comes seven years after the case was first brought by Gambia.

Dawda Jallow: The victory belongs to the Rohingya. They survived, they testified, and today they were believed.

Stephanie Sy: Rohingya survivors reacted after the decision.

Yasmin Ullah: It didn't feel real to me. I'm still kind of delirious from the decision that was read to us.

Stephanie Sy: Yasmin Ullah is the executive director of Rohingya Women's Collaborative Network.

Yasmin Ullah: It is also for them to feel like they can be heard, that their experience was real. It all validates the experience of the Rohingya.

Stephanie Sy: As the decision was announced in The Hague, Netherlands, thousands of miles away in Bangladesh, Rohingya refugees watched with anticipation.

Mohammad Rofik: Today, all courts recognize and, I mean, give the victory to the Rohingya community, not only Rohingya community. It is the victory of the whole community of the Myanmar. Those are suffering for a long time in the hands of the Myanmar military.

Stephanie Sy: The Rohingya are a Muslim minority from Buddhist majority Myanmar. Almost a decade ago, Myanmar's military executed what it called clearance operations in Rakhine state in response to a Rohingya insurgency that killed more than a dozen officers. The military burned entire villages, systematically raped victims, and, by conservative estimates, killed nearly 7,000 Rohingyas.

Hosna Ara: I have five children. One daughter was thrown in the fire by soldiers, and two are missing. I left my native village with my two children. But before I left, three soldiers entered my house and raped me. At the time, I was bleeding and I was crying. Then the military caught my youngest child and threw her in the fire. Another soldier beat me with a gun, and I continued to cry.

Stephanie Sy: 700,000 Rohingya civilians fled in the immediate aftermath to Bangladesh. But as the atrocities continued, more than 1.2 million Rohingya refugees left Myanmar.

Sayed Ullah: We are satisfied. So, what can we do in the future? We are satisfied, but yet we can't go back home.

Stephanie Sy: While today's ruling gives recognition, many are now wondering what comes next. To unpack what the genocide verdict means for international law and the future of the Rohingya people, we turn now to Rutgers law professor Adil Haque, author of "Law and Morality at War." Mr. Haque, thank you so much for joining the "NewsHour." Before we dive into what led the court to make this decision, I want to get into what those 1.2 million displaced Rohingya people can now expect. Can they expect reparations? Can they expect restitution? Is there a safe way for them to go home?

Adil Haque: Thanks very much for having me. So, certainly, that is what the court has ordered, restitution and compensation, to the extent that the Rohingya can return to their homes, they must be returned to their homes, and monetary compensation must be offered where interest cannot be repaired. That process will take several years to determine the form and amount of restitution and compensation. And then we have to see if Myanmar will comply. The United Kingdom has already called a meeting of the U.N. Security Council to hopefully support the court's orders and to ensure that Myanmar complies with those obligations. And then we have to wait and see if Myanmar does, in fact, do what it must do.

Stephanie Sy: The military -- the junta that rules Myanmar has not responded at all to the court. Have they cooperated at all in this process? Is there any reason to believe that the Rohingya will have a pathway to go back?

Adil Haque: So, the government of Myanmar has participated in the proceedings from the beginning, both under the prior government and now under the military government. So that creates some hope that the new government will comply with the court's directives and will comply with their legal obligations. Hopefully, the new government does not want to be a pariah or an outcast. They want to be a member of the international community and rejoin it, despite the terrible acts they have committed.

Stephanie Sy: As you mentioned, the United Kingdom's Foreign Office did issue a very harsh statement condemning Myanmar, calling for more sanctions. They are also dismissing the country's defense attache from the U.K. But other than that, we haven't heard much international response. Would you expect the U.N. Security Council to do anything? Would you expect any further international pressure?

Adil Haque: I certainly hope so. I certainly think that the United Kingdom, France and other -- some of the elected members of the Security Council will push for that. And then we have to wait and see what the United States, Russia and China, how they will do. But, certainly, states can take action outside of the Security Council, although it's less than ideal. There are other fora where they can coordinate their efforts to try to ensure that Myanmar does what it can, though it certainly can't undo what it has done, but perhaps offer something to its victims.

Stephanie Sy: How did Gambia, a third-party country that is not directly involved in this conflict in any way, manage to pull off this legal victory? Genocide is notoriously difficult to prove and prosecute.

Adil Haque: Thanks. Well, first, the Gambia did something quite extraordinary. It brought a case under the Genocide Convention on behalf of a minority group in another state. And the court, in an earlier proceeding, said that this is proper, this is something that states can do under the Genocide Convention. And that really opens the door to whole new pathways for accountability, that it was not clear were available before this case. So that's really to the credit of the Gambia. As for how they were able to achieve this result, it really turns on the evidence that they were able to present to the court, not only witness testimony, but relying heavily on UN fact-finding mission reports and independent investigative mechanism reports. And these really documented many of the atrocities that you described earlier, the mass killing, the commission of sexual violence on a large scale, the destruction of homes, mass displacement. And it was from all of that conduct that the court was able to infer genocidal intent to destroy a substantive...

Stephanie Sy: Sorry, Adil, the U.S. has expressed concern. This is a controversial decision in some quarters, because the U.S. has always feared that a decision like this would lower the threshold for proving genocide. Does this judgment do that? And what could it portend for other genocide cases before this court, including the one that South Africa has brought against Israel, as it relates to the war in Gaza?

Adil Haque: So, no, this decision does not change the court's interpretation of genocide or the applicable standard of proof. The standard remains very high. Genocide must be proven by fully convincing evidence and must be the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence. But in this case, the court found that, indeed, this is the only reasonable inference, and Myanmar's alternative theories of the case were simply not credible.

Stephanie Sy: That is Adil Haque, the author of "Law and Morality at War," joining us. Thank you for your insights.

Adil Haque: Thank you for having me.

SOURCE: PBS NewsHour, Nov. 19, 2026

Thousands of U.S. judges who broke laws or oaths remained on the bench
In the past dozen years, state and local judges have repeatedly escaped public accountability for misdeeds that have victimized thousands. Nine of 10 kept their jobs, a Reuters investigation found – including an Alabama judge who unlawfully jailed hundreds of poor people, many of them Black, over traffic fines.

By MICHAEL BERENS and JOHN SHIFFMAN in MONTGOMERY, ALABAMA Filed June 30, 2020, noon GMT
Judge Les Hayes once sentenced a single mother to 496 days behind bars for failing to pay traffic tickets. The sentence was so stiff it exceeded the jail time Alabama allows for negligent homicide.

Marquita Johnson, who was locked up in April 2012, says the impact of her time in jail endures today. Johnson’s three children were cast into foster care while she was incarcerated. One daughter was molested, state records show. Another was physically abused.

“Judge Hayes took away my life and didn’t care how my children suffered,” said Johnson, now 36. “My girls will never be the same.”

Fellow inmates found her sentence hard to believe. “They had a nickname for me: The Woman with All the Days,” Johnson said. “That’s what they called me: The Woman with All the Days. There were people who had committed real crimes who got out before me.”

In 2016, the state agency that oversees judges charged Hayes with violating Alabama’s code of judicial conduct. According to the Judicial Inquiry Commission, Hayes broke state and federal laws by jailing Johnson and hundreds of other Montgomery residents too poor to pay fines. Among those jailed: a plumber struggling to make rent, a mother who skipped meals to cover the medical bills of her disabled son, and a hotel housekeeper working her way through college.

Hayes, a judge since 2000, admitted in court documents to violating 10 different parts of the state’s judicial conduct code. One of the counts was a breach of a judge’s most essential duty: failing to “respect and comply with the law."

Despite the severity of the ruling, Hayes wasn’t barred from serving as a judge. Instead, the judicial commission and Hayes reached a deal. The former Eagle Scout would serve an 11-month unpaid suspension. Then he could return to the bench.

Until he was disciplined, Hayes said in an interview with Reuters, “I never thought I was doing something wrong.”

This week, Hayes is set to retire after 20 years as a judge. In a statement to Reuters, Hayes said he was “very remorseful” for his misdeeds.

Community activists say his departure is long overdue. Yet the decision to leave, they say, should never have been his to make, given his record of misconduct.

“He should have been fired years ago,” said Willie Knight, pastor of North Montgomery Baptist Church. “He broke the law and wanted to get away with it. His sudden retirement is years too late.”

Hayes is among thousands of state and local judges across America who were allowed to keep positions of extraordinary power and prestige after violating judicial ethics rules or breaking laws they pledged to uphold, a Reuters investigation found.

Judges have made racist statements, lied to state officials and forced defendants to languish in jail without a lawyer – and then returned to the bench, sometimes with little more than a rebuke from the state agencies overseeing their conduct.

Recent media reports have documented failures in judicial oversight in South Carolina, Louisiana and Illinois. Reuters went further.

In the first comprehensive accounting of judicial misconduct nationally, Reuters identified and reviewed 1,509 cases from the last dozen years – 2008 through 2019 – in which judges resigned, retired or were publicly disciplined following accusations of misconduct. In addition, reporters identified another 3,613 cases from 2008 through 2018 in which states disciplined wayward judges but kept hidden from the public key details of their offenses – including the identities of the judges themselves.

All told, 9 of every 10 judges were allowed to return to the bench after they were sanctioned for misconduct, Reuters determined. They included a California judge who had sex in his courthouse chambers, once with his former law intern and separately with an attorney; a New York judge who berated domestic violence victims; and a Maryland judge who, after his arrest for driving drunk, was allowed to return to the bench provided he took a Breathalyzer test before each appearance.

The news agency’s findings reveal an “excessively” forgiving judicial disciplinary system, said Stephen Gillers, a law professor at New York University who writes about judicial ethics. Although punishment short of removal from the bench is appropriate for most misconduct cases, Gillers said, the public “would be appalled at some of the lenient treatment judges get” for substantial transgressions.

Among the cases from the past year alone:

In Utah, a judge texted a video of a man’s scrotum to court clerks. He was reprimanded but remains on the bench.

In Indiana, three judges attending a conference last spring got drunk and sparked a 3 a.m. brawl outside a White Castle fast-food restaurant that ended with two of the judges shot. Although the state supreme court found the three judges had “discredited the entire Indiana judiciary,” each returned to the bench after a suspension.

In Texas, a judge burst in on jurors deliberating the case of a woman charged with sex trafficking and declared that God told him the defendant was innocent. The offending judge received a warning and returned to the bench. The defendant was convicted after a new judge took over the case.

“There are certain things where there should be a level of zero tolerance,” the jury foreman, Mark House, told Reuters. The judge should have been fined, House said, and kicked off the bench. “There is no justice, because he is still doing his job.”

Judicial misconduct specialists say such behavior has the potential to erode trust in America’s courts and, absent tough consequences, could give judges license to behave with impunity.

“When you see cases like that, the public starts to wonder about the integrity and honesty of the system,” said Steve Scheckman, a lawyer who directed Louisiana’s oversight agency and served as deputy director of New York’s. “It looks like a good ol’ boys club.”

That’s how local lawyers viewed the case of a longtime Alabama judge who concurrently served on the state’s judicial oversight commission. The judge, Cullman District Court’s Kim Chaney, remained on the bench for three years after being accused of violating the same nepotism rules he was tasked with enforcing on the oversight commission. In at least 200 cases, court records show, Judge Chaney chose his own son to serve as a court-appointed defense lawyer for the indigent, enabling the younger Chaney to earn at least $105,000 in fees over two years.

In February, months after Reuters repeatedly asked Chaney and the state judicial commission about those cases, he retired from the bench as part of a deal with state authorities to end the investigation.

Tommy Drake, the lawyer who first filed a complaint against Chaney in 2016, said he doubts the judge would have been forced from the bench if Reuters hadn’t examined the case.

“You know the only reason they did anything about Chaney is because you guys started asking questions,” Drake said. “Otherwise, he’d still be there.”

Bedrock of American justice

State and local judges draw little scrutiny even though their courtrooms are the bedrock of the American criminal justice system, touching the lives of millions of people every year.

The country’s approximately 1,700 federal judges hear 400,000 cases annually. The nearly 30,000 state, county and municipal court judges handle a far bigger docket: more than 100 million new cases each year, from traffic to divorce to murder. Their titles range from justice of the peace to state supreme court justice. Their powers are vast and varied – from determining whether a defendant should be jailed to deciding who deserves custody of a child.

Each U.S. state has an oversight agency that investigates misconduct complaints against judges. The authority of the oversight agencies is distinct from the power held by appellate courts, which can reverse a judge’s legal ruling and order a new trial. Judicial commissions cannot change verdicts. Rather, they can investigate complaints about the behavior of judges and pursue discipline ranging from reprimand to removal.

Few experts dispute that the great majority of judges behave responsibly, respecting the law and those who appear before them. And some contend that, when judges do falter, oversight agencies are effective in identifying and addressing the behavior. “With a few notable exceptions, the commissions generally get it right,” said Keith Swisher, a University of Arizona law professor who specializes in judicial ethics.

Others disagree. They note that the clout of these commissions is limited, and their authority differs from state to state. To remove a judge, all but a handful of states require approval of a panel that includes other judges. And most states seldom exercise the full extent of those disciplinary powers.

As a result, the system tends to err on the side of protecting the rights and reputations of judges while overlooking the impact courtroom wrongdoing has on those most affected by it: people like Marquita Johnson.

Reuters scoured thousands of state investigative files, disciplinary proceedings and court records from the past dozen years to quantify the personal toll of judicial misconduct. The examination found at least 5,206 people who were directly affected by a judge’s misconduct. The victims cited in disciplinary documents ranged from people who were illegally jailed to those subjected to racist, sexist and other abusive comments from judges in ways that tainted the cases.

The number is a conservative estimate. The tally doesn’t include two previously reported incidents that affected thousands of defendants and prompted sweeping reviews of judicial conduct.

“If we have a system that holds a wrongdoer accountable but we fail to address the victims, then we are really losing sight of what a justice system should be all about.”

Arthur Grim, retired judge

In Pennsylvania, the state examined the convictions of more than 3,500 teenagers sentenced by two judges. The judges were convicted of taking kickbacks as part of a scheme to fill a private juvenile detention center. In 2009, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court appointed senior judge Arthur Grim to lead a victim review, and the state later expunged criminal records for 2,251 juveniles. Grim told Reuters that every state should adopt a way to compensate victims of judicial misconduct.

“If we have a system that holds a wrongdoer accountable but we fail to address the victims, then we are really losing sight of what a justice system should be all about,” Grim said.

In another review underway in Ohio, state public defender Tim Young is scrutinizing 2,707 cases handled by a judge who retired in 2018 after being hospitalized for alcoholism. Mike Benza, a law professor at Case Western Reserve University whose students are helping identify victims, compared the work to current investigations into police abuse of power. “You see one case and then you look to see if it's systemic,” he said.

The review, which has been limited during the coronavirus pandemic, may take a year. But Young said the time-consuming task is essential because “a fundamental injustice may have been levied against hundreds or thousands of people.”

‘Special rules for judges’

Most states afford judges accused of misconduct a gentle kind of justice. Perhaps no state better illustrates the shortcomings of America’s system for overseeing judges than Alabama.

As in most states, Alabama’s nine-member Judicial Inquiry Commission is a mix of lawyers, judges and laypeople. All are appointed. Their deliberations are secret and they operate under some of the most judge-friendly rules in the nation.

Alabama’s rules make even filing a complaint against a judge difficult. The complaint must be notarized, which means that in theory, anyone who makes misstatements about the judge can be prosecuted for perjury. Complaints about wrongdoing must be made in writing; those that arrive by phone, email or without a notary stamp are not investigated, although senders are notified why their complaints have been summarily rejected. Anonymous written complaints are shredded.

These rules can leave lawyers and litigants fearing retaliation, commission director Jenny Garrett noted in response to written questions.

“It’s a ridiculous system that protects judges and makes it easy for them to intimidate anyone with a legitimate complaint,” said Sue Bell Cobb, chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court from 2007 to 2011. In 2009, she unsuccessfully championed changes to the process and commissioned an American Bar Association report that offered a scathing review of Alabama's rules.

In most other states, commission staff members can start investigating a judge upon receiving a phone call or email, even anonymous ones, or after learning of questionable conduct from a news report or court filing. In Alabama, staff will not begin an investigation without approval from the commission itself, which convenes about every seven weeks.

By rule, the commission also must keep a judge who is under scrutiny fully informed throughout an investigation. If a subpoena is issued, the judge receives a simultaneous copy, raising fears about witness intimidation. If a witness gives investigators a statement, the judge receives a transcript. In the U.S. justice system, such deference to individuals under investigation is extremely rare.

“It’s a ridiculous system that protects judges and makes it easy for them to intimidate anyone with a legitimate complaint.”

Sue Bell Cobb, former chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court

“Why the need for special rules for judges?” said Michael Levy, a Washington lawyer who has represented clients in high-profile criminal, corporate, congressional and securities investigations. “If judges think it’s fair and appropriate to investigate others for crimes or misconduct without providing those subjects or targets with copies of witness statements and subpoenas, why don’t judges think it’s fair to investigate judges in the same way?”

Alabama judges also are given an opportunity to resolve investigations confidentially. Reuters interviews and a review of Alabama commission records show the commission has met with judges informally at least 19 times since 2011 to offer corrective “guidance.” The identities of those judges remain confidential, as does the conduct that prompted the meetings. “Not every violation warrants discipline,” commission director Garrett said.

Since 2008, the commission has brought 21 public cases against judges, including Hayes, charging two this year.

Two of the best-known cases brought by the commission involved Roy Moore, who was twice forced out as chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court for defying federal court orders.

Another Alabama justice fared better in challenging a misconduct complaint, however. Tom Parker, first elected to the state’s high court in 2004, pushed back when the commission investigated him in 2015 for comments he made on the radio criticizing the U.S. Supreme Court's decision legalizing gay marriage.

Parker sued the commission in federal court, arguing the agency was infringing on his First Amendment rights. He won. Although the commission had dropped its investigation before the ruling, it was ordered to cover Parker’s legal fees: $100,000, or about a fifth of the agency’s total annual budget.

In 2018, the people of Alabama elected Parker chief justice.

These days, Parker told Reuters, Alabama judges and the agency that oversees them enjoy “a much better relationship” that’s less politically tinged. “How can I say it? It’s much more respectful between the commission and the judges now.”

Washington State 

SLAUGHTER HOUSE TEN

"The incoming crop of candidates gave credit to campaigning hard. We spent months knocking on doors."

Democrats Secure Supermajority in State House, but Fall Short in Senate

Nov. 19, 2026

The 10 Democrats who flipped state House seats from Republicans left to right: LD12's Stacy Willoughby, Ezequiel Morfin (LD14-2), Ben Christly (LD17-1), Randi Knott (LD18-1), Jenn Marie Strickling (LD25-2), David Berg (LD25-1), Chelsea Dimas (LD-14-1), Diana H. Perez (LD17-2), Deken Letinich (LD18-2), and LD26's Renee Hernandez Greenfield. 

Just about everything that could break Democrats' way in 2026 Washington State House races did, but the state Senate was a different story. Senate Democrats failed to make gains after Carolina Mejia's three-point election night lead evaporated in later returns in the Legislative District 35 race.

As a result, they'll have no pickups in the Senate, but stay at a comfortable 30-19 edge. That's still three seats short of a 2/3 supermajority.

Thanks to 10 seats they have tentatively flipped from Republicans, Democrats' advantage in the state House will grow from 59-39 to 69-29. That works out to 70% of seats, surpassing the 2/3 supermajority threshold, which makes overriding a governor's veto or passing a state constitutional amendment possible without Republican votes.

LD12-1: Stacy Willoughby
LD14-1: Chelsea Dimas
LD14-2: Ezequiel Morfin
LD17-1: Ben Christly
LD17-2: Diana H. Perez
LD18-1: Randi Knott
LD18-2: Deken Letinich
LD25-1: David Berg
LD25-2: Jenn Marie Strickling
LD26-2: Renee Hernandez Greenfield

Jenn Marie Strickling was the last Democrat to surpass her challenger, passing incumbent Rep. Cyndy Jacobsen in the second week of counting. As of November 17, Strickling was leading by 80 votes, with very few votes remaining to count. Pierce County estimates just 10 remaining ballots to count countywide, as of Tuesday.

"We feel extremely confident these results will hold," Strickling told The Urbanist Tuesday. "The blue wave this year reached all the way into the 25th, but what we're seeing here is also the result of a grassroots effort that's been years in the making. It’s the product of neighbors coming together, building relationships, and refusing to give up on their community."

If the lead stays near 0.14 percentage points (below the one quarter of one percent threshold), this would be headed to a manual recount, which is unlikely to change the outcome.

Jenn Marie Strickling took the lead on November 12, but the race remains razor close, with a 80-vote margin as of November 17. 

Why Democrats were able to win 10 seats in the state House while gaining none in the Senate was a bit of a fluke regarding which seats were up for election this year. Since state senators get four-year terms, only half of the districts are up in each even-year election.

Many key swing districts (shown in white) did not have state senate elections in 2026, which gave state Republicans a reprieve from suffering wider losses. (Washington Community Alliance)

Democrats' biggest gains were achieved in Legislative District 14, 17, 18, and 25, where they flipped two House seats (barring Strickling's narrow lead reversing). In each of those districts no Senate seats were up, but they will be in 2028.

With their pickups in 2026, Democrats have control of a contiguous swath of suburbia and cities from Olympia to Bellingham, encompassing the entire Seattle-Tacoma metropolitan area. (Washington Community Alliance)

Vancouver Democrat Adrian Cortes already flipped the LD18 seat in 2024, which was an early sign that Clark County's political alignment was shifting. On the other hand, LD14, LD17, and LD25 Senate seats are held by Republicans and will be key pickup opportunities.

LATEST: Denmark's parliament approved the Greenland defence agreement President Trump signed in September, 109 votes to 0, per its own tally on 19th November. It opens new United States defence areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, with terms still to be agreed.

The 109 were every member present in the 179 seat Folketing. Nobody voted against or abstained. Greenland's parliament, the Inatsisartut, approved it first, on 3rd November, by 16 votes to 0 with 7 abstentions.

Greenland's foreign minister told Danmarks Radio (DR), the Danish public broadcaster, that a diplomatic note went to Washington on Thursday and the agreement is now in force. The text says it takes effect on the date of that note. The Folketing notes that President Trump could conclude it for the United States without approval from Congress.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the agreement "modernizes the United States-Denmark-Greenland defense partnership" and bolsters the security of the United States and its allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). Ambassador Ken Howery called it "a tremendous accomplishment."

UPDATE on my 20th September post. I wrote that the Folketing would vote and then the Inatsisartut. The order ran the other way. Nuuk voted first and Copenhagen 16 days later.

That post also flagged 3 terms that United States officials were describing anonymously and that the Danish statement left out. All 3 are now in the signed text.

No state outside NATO may set up military installations or keep a lasting military presence in Greenland unless the parties agree. Investors from states outside NATO, its partner countries and the European Union may not gain control or significant influence in sensitive sectors, enforced through a Greenlandic screening law still to come. If Greenland becomes independent, Denmark and Greenland's government must ensure the new state commits to staying in NATO and takes on the agreement.

Access widens too. The United States may modernise and expand Pituffik Space Base. Its aircraft may overfly and land anywhere in Greenland, and its ships get submerged access to Greenland's territorial waters. The preamble names a Golden Dome missile defence system. Greenlandic firms are to get the commercial contracts for the defence areas as far as possible. The agreement has no end date.

It also moved fast. Signature on 22nd September to Danish consent took 58 days. The last defence agreement between the United States and Denmark, signed on 21st December 2023, took 558 days to enter into force.

What does not exist yet is a site plan. Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said on Thursday there had been no further talks with the United States on the 2 new bases since September, and that any request goes to a standing committee of the 3 parties, which meets in December. Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters he expects Washington to become more concrete about the 2 areas now.

The closest precedent is slow. The United States and the Philippines agreed 5 sites under their defence cooperation pact on 18th March 2016. Construction on the first project began on 17th April 2018, 760 days later.

My call, about 30 percent, is that Denmark, Greenland or the United States officially announces agreed terms for the Narsarsuaq or Mestersvig defence area by 30th June 2027.
I am wrong if no release from any of the 3 governments announces an agreed location, size or activity plan for either site by 30th June 2027.

text:
TRUMP QUESTIONS EUROPE'S BILLIONS FOR UKRAINE AFTER TALKS WITH PUTIN AND XI

Berlin rejects another Yalta as Washington challenges the cost of resisting Russian aggression.

Just hours after speaking with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, Donald Trump turned his attention to Europe's financial and military support for Ukraine. According to Politico, citing four European officials, the American president joined a telephone conversation with leaders attending the Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin and questioned why European governments continued pouring billions into Ukraine's defense.

Trump reportedly argued that too many people were dying while enormous sums were being spent on the conflict. He also told European leaders that Putin was serious about negotiating peace. The message raised a familiar question: what kind of peace is Moscow offering, and what would Ukraine be expected to surrender to obtain it?

The financial stakes are enormous. European Commission estimates indicate that Ukraine will require another €70 billion in military and budgetary assistance in 2027. Brussels has proposed a €45 billion loan to help cover those needs. For European governments, these figures represent more than another budgetary dispute. They concern Ukraine's ability to sustain its defense and Europe's capacity to influence the security arrangements that follow the war.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz responded by reaffirming Europe's commitment to supporting Kyiv for as long as necessary. He insisted that any meaningful peace negotiations must include both Ukraine and Europe, explicitly rejecting a return to the Yalta model, in which powerful states negotiate the future of smaller nations over their heads.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reinforced that position, promising continued assistance to Ukraine and sustained pressure on Russia. Her argument was that a durable and just settlement requires strength rather than concessions made under military pressure.

The disagreement reveals two contrasting approaches to ending the war. Trump is questioning the continuing financial cost and emphasizing Putin's stated willingness to negotiate. European leaders are emphasizing the conditions under which negotiations could produce a lasting settlement without compromising Ukrainian sovereignty.

And the central question remains unanswered: will peace mean the withdrawal of Russian aggression, or another agreement in which Ukraine is expected to pay for Putin's ambitions with its own territory?

Through 9 games this season he has produced 43 pressures, 6 sacks, 2 tackles for loss and 22 run stops. That work earns a 90.9 PFF grade, 4th of 496 qualifying FBS edge defenders, and puts him EDGE7 on this board's data ranking. His 2026 usage profile: wide-alignment edge (outside the tackle), flips sides (on the line 100% of snaps, outside T 99%, over T 1%, inside 0%). He plays with 3-star supporting-cast help (Rest of pass rush 14th pct · coverage behind him 95th pct), roughly average help for an FBS player. He plays for a Wisconsin team that is 6-4 through Nov. 14. His pass-rush skill (99th percentile) and get-off (99th) are both top-10% traits among FBS edge defenders, and that pairing is what separates him. Cheeks turns his speed into power, and we're big fans of his ability to drive offensive tackles backward before breaking free to reach the quarterback. His relentless pressure gives him the upside of a productive NFL pass rusher. We see a Round 3 starter-in-waiting, ideally as a wide-alignment edge rusher. We grade him as a Round 3 prospect: No. 84 on this board, against a consensus rank of No. 167.
